newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hospital workers join spreading strikes in S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Hospital workers join spreading strikes in S.Korea.

text.p: South Korean hospital workers walked out on strike on Friday, leaving only emergency care, as industrial action in protest at a new labour law spread from factories to key services.
Nurses and orderlies closed out-patient sections of 14 hospitals, including Seoul National University Hospital, the country's leading medical centre.

A general strike loomed after the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the biggest umbrella labour group, called out its 1.2 million members for an initial 24-hour action from 1.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) on Friday.

Some 150,000 workers from the half million-strong Korea Confederation of Trade Unions responded to a call from their leaders to down tools on Thursday, halting production at South Korea's largest car plant, Hyundai Motor, and major shipyards.
Workers at Daewoo Group's car plants and shipyards were set to walk out on Friday.
Vehicle production in South Korea is now virtually halted. Cars and ships are two of the country's biggest export items.

Journalists joined protests against the labour bill, staging sit-down demonstrations late on Thursday at the union offices of the Korea Broadcasting System. Broadcast unions were due to meet on Friday to decide on strike action.
Union wrath is aimed at a labour law railroaded through parliament on Thursday that gives employers the right to lay off surplus workers, introduce flexible working hours and replace strikers.
The government declared the strikes illegal, but although it has threatened "stern countermeasures" there was no sign yet of any crackdown on organised labour.
Huge worker rallies were planned on Friday on a concrete plaza near Seoul's new financial centre.

The Korea Employers' Federation was due to meet to discuss how to limit the damage from strikes that economists fear could drag on until well into next year, threatening already feeble corporate profits.

Export earnings have been savaged this year by plunging international prices for South Korea's key products. Stockpiles are now high, but protracted strikes could run them down and eventually exacerbate a ballooning trade deficit.
Public reaction to the strikers has so far been muted, but political analysts said sentiment could eventually turn against them if services were knocked out.
Seoul subway workers voted to strike from Saturday, a half day for most workers, threatening transport chaos for tens of thousands of commuters in the capital.

Opposition members of parliament staged an overnight sit- down protest against the government's shock tactics in ramming through the labour law and another controversial bill strengthening the powers of the once-notorious domestic spy agency.
They vowed to occupy the chamber until midnight on Saturday.
The bills were passed at a dawn session of the National Assembly attending only by ruling New Korea Party members.
Members of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics wore black ties on Friday to "mourn the death of democracy".
The opposition also declared it would challenge the new laws in the constitutional court.
